stem_html:
Sequencing the Denisovan genome required no skeleton, only a finger bone the size of a shirt button______ from it a team in Leipzig read a genome of higher quality than most of those then available for living humans.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • An inverted second clause hides its subject. “from it a team in Leipzig read” opens with a prepositional phrase, so the eye does not meet a subject immediately and the clause feels dependent.
  • The colon is nearly right. The second clause does elaborate on the first, which makes a colon defensible in feel and wrong in function here, because the first clause is not an announcement awaiting completion.
  • Bare “and” without a comma. Choice B joins two independent clauses with no punctuation at all, which reads fluently and is a run-on.

Why A is wrong A colon presents what follows as the completion of something the first clause has set up. Here the first clause is a complete statement about what was required, not a lead-in.

Why B is wrong Coordinating two independent clauses needs a comma before “and.” Without one the sentence runs on.

Why C is right Both halves are independent clauses and the second develops the first without a conjunction, which is exactly a semicolon's job.

Why D is wrong A comma between two independent clauses with no conjunction is a splice, and the inverted opening of the second clause is what disguises it.

stem_html:
The archaeologist Kathleen Kenyon, whose excavation of Jericho in the 1950s introduced the stratigraphic methods still used today______ published her results slowly enough that some of her conclusions were reported first by her students.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A comma opened this one, not a dash. The nonrestrictive clause beginning “whose excavation” is fenced by commas, so the fence has to close with a comma.
  • Twenty words of clause make the subject feel spent. By the blank a reader has forgotten that “Kathleen Kenyon” still has no verb, which is why omitting punctuation entirely feels acceptable.
  • Nothing after the blank can stand alone. “published her results slowly” is a predicate, so neither a semicolon nor a colon can precede it.

Why A is wrong A semicolon needs a complete clause on both sides, and the right side here is a bare predicate.

Why B is wrong A colon would introduce what follows as an explanation or list, and what follows is the sentence's own main verb.

Why C is wrong Leaving the interrupting clause unclosed runs it into the predicate, so the reader briefly takes “used today published” as a unit.

Why D is right It closes the pair of commas around the nonrestrictive clause that introduced the stratigraphic methods still used today, and lets the subject reach its verb.

stem_html:
Tidal power has an advantage no other renewable can claim______ its output is known years in advance, because the moon is not weather.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Two marks are grammatical and one is right. A semicolon would be legal here, so this question is decided by what the first clause promises rather than by clause structure alone.
  • “An advantage no other renewable can claim” is an announcement. It names something without saying what it is, so the reader is owed a completion, and that is a colon's specific work.
  • The comma reads naturally aloud. Spoken, the sentence has one pause at the blank, which is exactly what makes a splice hard to hear.

Why A is right The first clause promises an advantage and does not say what it is; the second delivers it. A colon marks that promise-and-payoff relation, which a semicolon leaves unstated.

Why B is wrong Grammatically permissible and weaker. A semicolon says the two clauses are related and stops there, discarding the announcement the first clause makes.

Why C is wrong Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone. The splice is well hidden because the sentence has a natural spoken pause in the same place.

Why D is wrong “and” needs a comma before it here, and even then it would coordinate the clauses as equals rather than delivering the advantage the first one announces.

stem_html:
Hedy Lamarr and George Antheil patented a frequency-hopping system in 1942______ the Navy shelved it, and the idea reached consumers only in the 1990s, in the radios that became Bluetooth.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The sentence already contains a comma-plus-conjunction. “, and the idea reached consumers” is doing that job later, so a second comma at the blank produces two different joins of the same weight.
  • Chronology invites a colon. What follows does continue the story, and a colon looks like the mark for “and then,” which it is not.
  • A dash plus a relative pronoun. Choice A turns the second clause into a modifier of “1942,” which is not what was shelved.

Why A is wrong “that” attaches the shelving to the nearest noun, 1942, producing a relative clause with the wrong antecedent and no main verb for the second half.

Why B is right Two independent clauses, closely related, with no conjunction between them. The semicolon also keeps the later comma-plus-and free to coordinate the two halves of the second clause.

Why C is wrong A splice. The clause after the blank has its own subject and verb, and no conjunction joins them.

Why D is wrong A colon would frame the Navy's decision as an explanation of the patent, and it is a subsequent event, not an unpacking of the first clause.

stem_html:
Because the manuscript's ink contains iron gall, which corrodes parchment over centuries______ conservators photograph each page under raking light before any treatment begins.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The sentence opens with “Because,” so the first half is dependent. A subordinate clause cannot sit on the left of a semicolon or a colon, however long it has grown.
  • Length imitates independence. By the blank the reader has passed a full clause inside the relative “which corrodes parchment over centuries,” and that clause is what makes the stronger marks feel available.

Why A is wrong A colon also requires an independent clause to its left. The embedded relative clause makes the left side sound complete without making it so.

Why B is wrong “and” would coordinate the subordinate clause with the main clause, which are not of the same kind, and it leaves the sentence with no main clause at all.

Why C is right A comma is the standard mark between an introductory subordinate clause and the main clause that follows it.

Why D is wrong A semicolon requires independent clauses on both sides, and “Because the manuscript's ink contains iron gall” cannot stand alone.

stem_html:
Widely regarded as the most complete Roman shipwreck yet found in the Adriatic, ______

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"it took divers three seasons to survey the Cape Stobreč wreck.","trap":"distant-antecedent"},{"letter":"B","content":"divers surveyed the Cape Stobreč wreck in three seasons.","trap":"modifier-attachment"},{"letter":"C","content":"the survey of the Cape Stobreč wreck took three seasons.","trap":"modifier-attachment"},{"letter":"D","content":"the Cape Stobreč wreck took divers three seasons to survey."}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The opening phrase describes exactly one thing. A shipwreck can be the most complete Roman shipwreck in the Adriatic; divers, a survey and an empty “it” cannot.
  • Choice C swaps one noun for a noun phrase built on it. “The survey of the wreck” contains the word wreck, which is enough to make the modifier feel attached, and the subject is still the survey.
  • Every choice is a good sentence alone. The error lives only in the join, so checking the choices in isolation cannot find it.

Why A is wrong “It” here is a placeholder with no antecedent, so the introductory phrase modifies nothing.

Why B is wrong It makes the divers the most complete Roman shipwreck in the Adriatic.

Why C is wrong The subject is the survey, not the wreck. A survey is not a shipwreck, however closely the phrase mentions one.

Why D is right The wreck is the subject, and the wreck is what the opening phrase describes. The rest of the sentence still reports how long the survey took.

stem_html:
The lab's protocol requires that every sample ______ logged within an hour of collection, a rule adopted after a batch of cores sat unlabeled over a holiday weekend.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “Requires that” takes the subjunctive. After verbs of demand the clause verb is the base form, which sounds wrong to an ear trained on ordinary agreement.
  • The singular subject invites “is.” “every sample” is singular, so the agreement instinct produces the wrong answer confidently.
  • A past-tense anecdote follows. The clause about the holiday weekend pulls toward a past-tense verb that belongs to the anecdote, not to the rule.

Why A is right The mandative subjunctive: after “requires that,” the verb is the base form regardless of the subject's number, so “every sample be logged.”

Why B is wrong Past tense, borrowed from the anecdote at the end of the sentence. The protocol is a standing requirement.

Why C is wrong The future turns a standing rule into a prediction, and the subjunctive is still what the governing verb demands.

Why D is wrong The indicative. It agrees correctly in number and still breaks the subjunctive that “requires that” governs.

stem_html:
Neither of the two surviving copies of the 1791 broadside ______ the printer's name, which is why the attribution rests entirely on the distinctive damage to one letter of the type.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “Neither” is the subject, not “copies.” The prepositional phrase “of the two surviving copies” contains a plural noun and the number two, and neither of them governs the verb.
  • Two choices hide their number in an auxiliary. “have carried” and “were carrying” are plural, and a reader checking the participle instead of the auxiliary misses it.

Why A is wrong Plural, agreeing with “copies” rather than with “Neither.”

Why B is right “Neither” takes a singular verb, and the simple present states a fact about the copies that still holds.

Why C is wrong Plural in the auxiliary, and the present perfect implies a change over time where a standing fact is meant.

Why D is wrong Plural and progressive, which describes something in the course of happening rather than a permanent property of the printed sheets.

stem_html:
The report notes that the flood barrier protected the hospital and the two schools behind it, but ______ came at the cost of directing water into the marsh that had absorbed the previous surge.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Three nouns and an action are all available. Before the blank sit the barrier, the hospital, the two schools and the act of protecting, so any bare pronoun has at least four possible antecedents.
  • A bare demonstrative feels precise and is not. “This” pointing at a whole preceding clause is common in speech and ambiguous on the page, which is why it is the most chosen wrong answer.
  • The plural is available too. “They” can reach back to the schools, which makes it read acceptably while saying something the sentence does not mean.

Why A is wrong Plural, so it points to the schools, which are what was protected rather than what carried a cost.

Why B is wrong “This” with no noun after it leaves the reader to decide whether the barrier, the protecting, or the whole situation came at a cost.

Why C is right The noun phrase names what came at a cost, and no other choice can distinguish the act of protecting from the structure that did it.

Why D is wrong “It” could be the barrier, the hospital or the marsh, and the sentence gives no way to choose.

stem_html:
By 2035, engineers expect that the tunnel's ventilation system ______ for more than fifty years without a full shutdown.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A future deadline with a span behind it. “By 2035” sets a point in the future and “for more than fifty years” measures backwards from it, which only one tense can express.
  • The simple future is the obvious answer and loses the span. “Will run for fifty years” describes a stretch starting now, not one completed by a future date.

Why A is wrong The present perfect measures the span as of now, and the sentence explicitly measures it as of 2035.

Why B is wrong The simple past puts the running wholly in the past and contradicts a sentence about what engineers expect.

Why C is wrong The simple future says the system will operate for fifty years starting from now, which would put the milestone well beyond 2035.

Why D is right The future perfect measures a completed span as of a future moment, which is what “By 2035 … for more than fifty years” requires.

stem_html:
Reading Ezra Pound's editorial marks on the manuscript of The Waste Land, one is struck less by his judgment than by his ______: whole passages are struck out with no suggestion of a replacement, as though the poem's shape were already visible to him and the cuts merely uncovered it.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The colon defines the blank. What follows is not that Pound cut a great deal but that he cut without hesitation or alternatives, which is a claim about confidence.
  • Severity is true and is not the contrast. The sentence sets the blank against “his judgment,” and harshness is a kind of judgment, so it fails the contrast the sentence is built on.
  • The literary-critical register. “Erudition” is a word one expects near Pound, and nothing in the sentence concerns learning.

Why A is right Passages struck out with no suggestion of a replacement, as though the shape of the poem were settled in advance, describe someone who does not doubt. Assurance names that, and it contrasts properly with judgment.

Why B is wrong Erudition is deep learning. The evidence offered is about how decisively he cut, not about what he knew.

Why C is wrong The cuts are severe, so this is half right, and severity is a species of judgment rather than the alternative to it the sentence promises.

Why D is wrong Caprice is the opposite of what the second clause describes: the cuts follow a shape Pound could already see, which is the reverse of whim.

stem_html:
The treaty's language was deliberately ______: each government could tell its own legislature that the disputed fishing rights had been preserved, and for eleven years neither found it useful to ask what the other had understood.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Unclear and usefully unclear are different. The sentence describes wording that lets two parties reach opposite readings and both be satisfied, which is more specific than obscurity.
  • “Provisional” collocates with treaties. The word belongs to the subject matter and not to the sentence, which says nothing about the agreement being temporary.
  • Eleven years is the tell. The arrangement held, so the language worked; a merely obscure text would have produced a dispute, not a decade of quiet.

Why A is wrong Concise concerns length. Nothing here turns on how short the treaty was.

Why B is right Elastic language stretches to cover incompatible readings, which is exactly why each government could tell its own legislature that the disputed fishing rights had been preserved.

Why C is wrong Obscure says the text is hard to understand. The point is that each side understood it perfectly and differently, and was content to leave it there.

Why D is wrong Provisional means temporary, and the sentence describes a settled text that lasted eleven years without renegotiation.

stem_html:
The dam's designers treated the river's sediment load as an ______ nuisance: the reservoir would trap it, the delta downstream would starve, and both effects were entered in the plans as costs rather than as questions to be reopened.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “Entered in the plans” settles it. Anything written into the plans was foreseen, which eliminates the most tempting choice outright.
  • “Nuisance” primes a word about difficulty. The blank is about the designers' stance toward the problem, not about how hard the problem is.

Why A is wrong Nothing in the sentence describes the nuisance growing over time.

Why B is wrong Directly contradicted: both effects were entered in the plans, so they were anticipated rather than unforeseen.

Why C is right The designers saw the sediment problem, wrote it down, and declined to reconsider it. Acknowledged captures being recognized and set aside, which is what “as costs rather than as questions” describes.

Why D is wrong Intractable says the problem could not be solved. The passage says it was not treated as a question at all, which is a choice rather than an impossibility.

stem_html:
A team argued that the medieval fish trade reached inland England earlier than the documents suggest, on the grounds that cod bones from a York site dated to 1050 carry a chemical signature typical of the Arctic. A critic responded that the signature also occurs in cod from the southern North Sea during unusually cold decades, and that the eleventh century included several.

Which finding, if true, would most directly counter the critic's response?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"The chemical signature of Arctic cod has been measured in modern specimens from several fishing grounds.","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"B","content":"Documents from the twelfth century record a substantial trade in dried cod reaching inland markets.","trap":"true-but-irrelevant"},{"letter":"C","content":"Cold decades in the eleventh century were more frequent than previously estimated.","trap":"reversed-relationship"},{"letter":"D","content":"Cod bones from a coastal site fifty kilometers from York, dated to the same decade, carry the southern North Sea signature rather than the Arctic one."}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The critic offers an alternative source, not an objection to the chemistry. Countering it means showing local cod of that date did not carry the Arctic signature, which is a comparison, not a measurement.
  • Later documents are the wrong century. C confirms trade in the twelfth century, and the claim under dispute is about 1050.
  • Strengthening the objection by accident. D makes cold decades more common, which makes the critic's explanation more available, not less.

Why A is wrong Modern reference measurements establish that the method works. The dispute is about which population the medieval fish came from.

Why B is wrong Trade a century later is consistent with both accounts of the 1050 bones and settles nothing about them.

Why C is wrong More cold decades makes the critic's alternative more likely, which is the opposite of countering it.

Why D is right The critic's account requires that cod from the southern North Sea during unusually cold decades could look Arctic. A shows contemporaneous local cod carrying the southern signature instead, so the York bones cannot be explained as local fish in a cold decade.

stem_html:
Researchers compared two reading programs in a district, measuring comprehension gains after one year. Program A produced larger average gains, but the team concluded that Program B is the better choice for the district's lowest-scoring readers.

Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support the team's conclusion?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"In the lowest quartile Program B produced a gain of 12 points against Program A's 4, the only quartile in which B's advantage exceeded two points."},{"letter":"B","content":"Program B's gains were more consistent across quartiles, ranging only from 6 to 12 points.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"C","content":"Averaged across all four quartiles, Program A and Program B produced gains of 9 and 8.25 points respectively.","trap":"true-but-irrelevant"},{"letter":"D","content":"Program A produced a gain of 15 points in the highest quartile, the largest gain recorded for either program.","trap":"wrong-part-of-passage"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The conclusion is about one quartile. Anything averaged over all four, however carefully computed, cannot support a claim restricted to the lowest-scoring readers.
  • The largest number on the chart belongs to the other program. A reports it accurately and argues for the conclusion's opposite.
  • Consistency is a different virtue. C is true and would support “B is more even,” not “B is better for the weakest readers.”

Why A is right The conclusion names Program B the better choice for the district's lowest-scoring readers, and this is the only choice that reads that quartile: 12 against 4, a gap that appears nowhere else. It also notes that the advantage is confined to Q1, which is what makes the restriction to the lowest quartile the right conclusion rather than a general preference.

Why B is wrong Consistency across quartiles is a property of Program B and not a reason to prefer it for one particular group.

Why C is wrong The averages are close and slightly favor A. They are also exactly the summary the conclusion refuses to be based on.

Why D is wrong It reports Program A's best result, in the quartile the conclusion is not about, and it supports choosing A rather than B.

stem_html:
In Mariama Bâ's epistolary novel So Long a Letter, the narrator addresses a friend who never replies within the text. A critic argues that the friend's silence is what allows the narrator to revise her own account as she writes.

Which quotation from the novel would most directly support the critic's claim?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"“I have written to you every evening for thirty days, and I have not once been interrupted.”","trap":"wrong-part-of-passage"},{"letter":"B","content":"“I told you last week that I had forgiven him; reading that over, I find I had only decided to stop saying otherwise.”"},{"letter":"C","content":"“You would understand this better than anyone, which is why I write to you and not to my sister.”","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"D","content":"“The house is quiet now that the children have gone, and the mangoes have come in early.”","trap":"true-but-irrelevant"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The claim has two parts and only one is easy to illustrate. Silence is easy to find; the revision that silence permits is the part the quotation has to show.
  • The literal restatement is the trap. D says outright that nobody interrupts, which illustrates the silence and shows no revision at all.
  • Choosing the addressee is not revising the account. B explains why she writes to this friend rather than what the writing does to her story.

Why A is wrong It documents the silence and stops there. The critic's claim is about what the silence enables, and an uninterrupted month by itself shows no change of mind.

Why B is right The narrator quotes her own earlier letter and corrects it: what she had called forgiveness she now calls having stopped saying otherwise. That is the silence allowing the narrator to revise her own account as she writes, which is what the critic's claim requires.

Why C is wrong It explains the choice of correspondent. Nothing in it shows the narrator changing anything she has said.

Why D is wrong Domestic detail. It neither establishes the silence nor shows any revision.

stem_html:
An urban planner claimed that removing minimum parking requirements lowers the cost of new apartments. She pointed to a city where, in the three years after such a reform, newly permitted buildings included 40 percent fewer parking spaces per unit and advertised rents 8 percent below the metropolitan average.

Which finding, if true, would most seriously weaken the planner's claim?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"The metropolitan average rent rose during the same three years.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"B","content":"Parking spaces are expensive to build, often costing tens of thousands of dollars each.","trap":"reversed-relationship"},{"letter":"C","content":"Buildings permitted after the reform were concentrated in neighborhoods where rents were already 9 percent below the metropolitan average before the reform."},{"letter":"D","content":"Some buildings permitted after the reform still included more parking than the old minimum required.","trap":"true-but-irrelevant"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A comparison to the wrong baseline. The claim rests on new buildings being cheaper than the metropolitan average. If those buildings sit where rents were already lower, the comparison shows location rather than reform.
  • The choice that explains the mechanism strengthens the claim. D says parking is expensive, which is the planner's reasoning restated.
  • Exceptions are not counterexamples. B notes that some developers built extra parking anyway, which is compatible with an average fall of 40 percent.

Why A is wrong A rising metropolitan average is the benchmark moving, and since the comparison is a percentage below that average, this does not by itself undo it.

Why B is wrong This is the planner's own premise, that parking costs money to build, and it supports rather than weakens the claim.

Why C is right The planner's evidence is that the new buildings advertised rents 8 percent below the metropolitan average. A supplies a pre-existing difference of the same size, so that gap is what those neighborhoods looked like before the reform. The evidence no longer distinguishes the reform's effect from where the building happened.

Why D is wrong A minority of buildings exceeding the old minimum is consistent with a large average reduction and says nothing about rents.

stem_html:
The conventional account of the Antonine Plague relies on a handful of literary sources, most of them written decades after the outbreak. Papyrological evidence from Egyptian villages has been used to fill the gap, and tax rolls do show sharp population declines in the 160s. ______ those rolls record taxpayers rather than residents, so a village whose survivors fled a tax district would look depopulated whether or not anyone had died.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Two sentences of support, then a withdrawal. The tax rolls are introduced as filling the gap, and the last sentence explains why they may not.
  • “Indeed” intensifies whatever came before. It would present the taxpayer objection as further confirmation of the decline.
  • The final clause has the shape of a conclusion. “so a village … would look depopulated” invites a causal transition, and the causation is inside the sentence, not between the sentences.

Why A is wrong Causal, and the wrong direction: the objection does not follow from the population decline, it questions whether the decline is what the rolls show.

Why B is wrong The taxpayer point is not an instance of the sharp decline; it is a competing explanation of the same record.

Why C is wrong Confirmatory. It would say the taxpayer point supports the reading of the tax rolls, when it undercuts it.

Why D is right The last sentence removes the evidential force of the rolls by pointing out what they actually count. That is a contrast with the sentence before it, which offered them as evidence.

stem_html:
Coral restoration often works by fragmenting fast-growing branching species and outplanting the pieces, which produces visible cover within a few years. Reef function, though, depends heavily on massive slow-growing corals that provide the structure fish shelter in. ______ a reef can be judged a restoration success by percentage cover while offering less habitat than it did before the bleaching.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The paradox in the last sentence is the effect, not a contrast. It follows from the mismatch between what restoration grows and what function requires, which the two preceding sentences establish together.
  • A surprising conclusion feels contrastive. “Success by cover, less habitat” sounds like a reversal, so a contrastive transition is the most chosen error; the reversal is inside the sentence.

Why A is right Fast-growing fragments produce cover, and function depends on slow-growing corals. The consequence is a reef that scores well on cover and shelters less, which is what the final sentence states.

Why B is wrong “Instead” substitutes one thing for another. Nothing is being replaced here; a consequence is being drawn.

Why C is wrong Comparative, and there is no second case to be like the first.

Why D is wrong Concessive. It would set the last sentence against the previous one, and the last sentence is what the previous one implies.

stem_html:
Economists studying minimum wage increases once relied on comparisons between states, which are confounded by everything else that differs between them. Card and Krueger's 1994 study instead compared fast-food restaurants on opposite sides of a single state line. ______ the design does not eliminate confounding entirely: a state that raises its wage may be a state whose economy is already growing, and the border does not separate two economies so much as cut one in half.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • An improvement is being praised and then qualified. The border design is offered as better than state comparisons, and the last sentence limits how much better.
  • “Therefore” makes the limitation follow from the improvement. The sentence's internal “so” and colon give it the cadence of a derivation, which is the bait.
  • “In particular” promises a specific case of the previous claim. What follows is not an instance of the design but a limit on it.

Why A is wrong It signals elaboration of what was just said, and the sentence introduces an objection instead.

Why B is right The concessive transition marks a qualification: the border design is an improvement, and it still leaves confounding in place. That is precisely the relation between the last two sentences.

Why C is wrong Causal and backwards. The design's remaining weakness does not follow from its adoption; it survives it.

Why D is wrong Comparative. It would make the limitation parallel to the study rather than a caveat about it.

stem_html:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Roman concrete harbors at Caesarea have survived two thousand years in seawater.
  • Modern marine concrete is typically designed for a service life of 50 to 100 years.
  • Roman concrete used volcanic ash, which reacts with seawater to form aluminous tobermorite.
  • That reaction continues over centuries, filling cracks as they form.
  • Roman concrete is far weaker than modern concrete in initial compressive strength.

The student wants to explain why Roman concrete outlasts modern concrete in seawater without overstating its advantages. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"The harbors at Caesarea have survived two thousand years in seawater, far longer than the service life for which modern marine concrete is designed.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"B","content":"Roman concrete is superior to modern concrete: harbors at Caesarea have stood in seawater for two thousand years, while modern marine concrete is designed to last 50 to 100 years.","trap":"too-extreme"},{"letter":"C","content":"Although Roman concrete is far weaker than modern concrete at the outset, its volcanic ash reacts with seawater over centuries to form aluminous tobermorite, filling cracks as they form."},{"letter":"D","content":"Roman concrete used volcanic ash, and modern marine concrete is typically designed for a service life of 50 to 100 years.","trap":"out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The goal has a brake in it. “Without overstating” is a constraint the choices are built to violate, and the most rhetorically satisfying choice violates it hardest.
  • The durability comparison is not the explanation. D states the outcome and never says why, which leaves “explain why” unmet.
  • Two facts side by side are not a mechanism. C names the ash and the modern service life without connecting them.

Why A is wrong It reports the durability gap accurately and explains nothing about what causes it.

Why B is wrong “Superior” overstates exactly what the notes qualify: Roman concrete is far weaker in initial compressive strength. It also gives the outcome rather than the reason.

Why C is right It concedes the weakness first, which is what keeps the claim from overstating, and then gives the mechanism that produces the longevity: a reaction that continues over centuries, filling cracks as they form.

Why D is wrong One fact about each material with nothing joining them. The volcanic ash is left doing no work.

  • Saturn itself is about 4.5 billion years old.
  • The mass estimate depends on separating the gravity of the rings from that of the planet.

The student wants to present the age finding and note a limitation of the method. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

Traps in this question

  • Two requirements, and three choices meet one. The finding without the caveat, or the caveat without the finding, both read as complete answers.
  • The striking contrast crowds out the method. C's 4.5 billion against 100 million is the memorable line and carries no limitation at all.
  • An invented rationale. D turns the limitation into the reason for the mission, which the notes do not say.

Why A is wrong It describes the orbits and stops before the result, so neither the finding nor the limitation appears.

Why B is wrong The age contrast without the mass measurement or the caveat. It states a conclusion with no method attached.

Why C is wrong It presents the limitation as the mission's motivation, an inference the notes do not support, and it never gives the age finding.

Why D is right It gives the measurement, the age it implies, and then the dependency that limits it, in that order. Both halves of the goal are met and neither is buried.

stem_html:
A pharmacologist tested whether a compound slows tumor growth by blocking a particular enzyme. In mice with normal tumors the compound slowed growth substantially. In mice whose tumors had been engineered to lack the enzyme entirely, the compound slowed growth by about the same amount. These results suggest that the compound's effect ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"operates through some target other than the enzyme, since removing the enzyme did not diminish it."},{"letter":"B","content":"is smaller than the experiment's design can detect.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"C","content":"would disappear if the dose were reduced.","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"D","content":"depends on blocking the enzyme, since the effect appeared in both groups.","trap":"reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The identical result is the finding, and it feels like confirmation. “It worked in both groups” reads as a success for the hypothesis, and it is the evidence that refutes it.
  • A knockout is a control, not a replicate. If the enzyme were the route, removing it should have removed the effect.
  • Choices about dose and detection appear rigorous. Neither is varied in the experiment described.

Why A is right In tumors engineered to lack the enzyme entirely the compound slowed growth by about the same amount, so whatever the compound does, it does not require the enzyme to do it. Some other target is the only account left.

Why B is wrong The effect was substantial in both groups, so detection is not the problem.

Why C is wrong Dose is not varied anywhere in the experiment, so nothing in the results speaks to it.

Why D is wrong It reverses the logic of the control. An effect that survives the removal of the supposed target cannot be running through that target.

stem_html:
Two lakes in the same watershed received identical amounts of road salt over a decade. In the deeper lake, chloride concentrations at the surface returned to background levels each spring, while concentrations near the bottom rose steadily year after year. In the shallow lake, chloride rose and fell together at all depths. The difference indicates that the deeper lake ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "received more road salt than the researchers recorded.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "does not mix completely from top to bottom, so salt reaching the bottom is not carried back to the surface."}, {"letter": "C", "content": "has a larger surface area than the shallow lake.", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "loses chloride to groundwater more quickly than the shallow lake does.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The premise is equality of input. Both lakes received identical amounts, so any choice that explains the difference by unequal salt contradicts the setup.
  • Depth is offered as a description and is really the mechanism. The pattern — clean at the surface, accumulating at the bottom — is what stratification looks like.
  • Faster loss cannot explain accumulation. D would predict lower bottom concentrations, not a steady rise.

Why A is wrong The passage states the lakes received identical amounts of road salt, so this rejects a given rather than explaining the result.

Why B is right Surface water clearing every spring while bottom water accumulates is exactly what happens when the two layers do not exchange. The shallow lake, mixing throughout, shows the same signal at all depths.

Why C is wrong Surface area is never mentioned and would not by itself produce a difference between the top and the bottom of the same lake.

Why D is wrong Losing chloride faster predicts falling concentrations, and the deep lake's bottom concentrations rose steadily year after year.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2015 essay on public statistics.

Every few years someone proposes replacing the unemployment rate with a broader measure, one that counts discouraged workers and the involuntarily part-time. The broader measures already exist; the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes six of them every month, and has for decades. What the proposals are really asking is which number the evening news should read out, and that is a question about attention rather than about measurement.

Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"It proposes a specific broader measure for the Bureau to adopt.","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"B","content":"It explains the method by which discouraged workers are counted.","trap":"wrong-part-of-passage"},{"letter":"C","content":"It supplies the evidence that recasts the proposals as being about prominence rather than about data."},{"letter":"D","content":"It concedes that the current unemployment rate is inadequate.","trap":"reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The sentence looks like a fact and works as a refutation. Its two clauses quietly remove the premise of the proposals, and the sentence after it says what is therefore left.
  • Existence is not endorsement. Reporting that six measures are published does not concede that the headline one is inadequate.
  • The word “discouraged” appears earlier. That makes a choice about counting methods feel supported, and no method is described anywhere.

Why A is wrong No measure is recommended. Six are said to exist already.

Why B is wrong The sentence gives a count and a publisher, not a counting method.

Why C is right The sentence establishes that the broader measures already exist and are published monthly, which is what allows the final sentence to redescribe the proposals as being about which number gets read out. It is the hinge between the proposal and the reinterpretation.

Why D is wrong It concedes nothing about adequacy. It reports what is published, and the essay's point is that publication is not the issue.
